name: inauguration

attributes.attribute: a Celtic ritual in which a chosen man became king by marrying the goddess of the land
the feast of inauguration celebrating the marriage of the goddess of sovereignty and her chosen king
sacred taboos and promises that bounded a Celtic king's life

sources: Brenneman, Walter, and Mary Brenneman. Crossing the Circle at the Holy Wells of Ireland. Charlottesville: University of Virginia Press, 1995.
Green, Miranda. Symbol and Image in Celtic Religious Art. London: Routledge, 1989.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Inauguration was a Celtic ritual of kingship. Evidence of its form in Celtic Ireland is strong. The king was not an absolute ruler. Poets chose him, often by complex divination, and sometimes by feats arms. He then married the goddess of the land. The banais ríghe was the feast of inauguration. It celebrated the marriage of the goddess of sovereignty with her chosen king. The rite took place on a sacred hill such as Tara or at a holy well. After the rite the king followed many rules. If he pleased the goddess, she granted abundant food and fine weather. If he failed, famine and disease fell on the land, and he lost office. Sacred taboos, called geasa, bound his life.
objective: Document the Celtic ritual of kingly inauguration.
key_results: Record how poets chose the king, by divination or feats of arms.
Explain the banais righ and the marriage to the goddess of the land.
Note the sacred taboos, called geasa, that bound the king.
